The results of the replication study
      largely confirmed the original safety climate model. However, in addition to indirect effects, direct links
      between safety climate and actual safety behavior were found.
decisions.location: Abstract, p. 143, lines 34-36 (see also Section 5.3, p. 150, lines 474-484, and Section 7, p. 153, lines 636-645)
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding record 'mixed'. The paper tests two core hypotheses from Griffin and Neal's (2000) [11] model: the higher-order five-factor structure of safety climate (Hypothesis 1) and full mediation by safety knowledge and safety motivation between safety climate and safety performance (Hypothesis 2). In Section 5.3 (p. 150) and Section 7 (p. 153), the authors state an explicit overall verdict that the model was 'partially validated' / 'partly confirmed': Hypothesis 1 was replicated, whereas in explicit contrast to Griffin and Neal's original full-mediation model [11], safety climate also exerted significant direct effects on safety compliance and safety participation (partial rather than full mediation on Hypothesis 2).

decisions.quote:
This paper attempts to replicate a safety climate model originally tested in Australia to assess its applicability
      in a different context: namely, across production workers in 22 medium-sized metal processing organizations
      in Austria. The model postulates that safety knowledge and safety motivation mediate the relation between
      safety climate on the one hand and safety compliance and participation on the other. Self-report data from
      1075 employees were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM).
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree on 'replication'. The authors collected new survey data from 1,075 production workers across 22 Austrian metal processing companies using German translations of Griffin and Neal's (2000) [11] items to re-test the published safety climate model in a new sample.
